841.title: The king who saw heaven and hell
841.hook: King Nemi is shown both, and returns to govern well (Jataka 541)
841.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching describes heavens and hells as places beings pass through according to their deeds, not as final destinations; the Nimi story is told to show how actions shape what follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sama, shot at the river, thinking first of his blind parents. Your line: who will bring them water. Today, a new week, and a king given a ride through other worlds.

A chariot comes down out of the sky for a king. King Nimi of Mithila gives freely and keeps the precepts, and the story says even the gods start talking about him. Sakka, their king, wants to meet him, so he sends his own charioteer, Matali, to bring Nimi up. On the way, Matali asks a question: which road would you like to take?
screen: `A CHARIOT FROM THE SKY.` → `THE GODS TALK OF NIMI.` → `WHICH ROAD FIRST?`

segments.voice: Nimi asks to see both. Matali drives him past the hells first, and at each one Nimi asks the same question: what did these beings do? Matali answers, deed by deed: cruelty, cheating, harm done to the weak. The tale doesn't linger for horror's sake. It's a map of where actions lead. Then the chariot rises, and Nimi sees mansions of light. Again he asks what these beings did, and again the answer is deeds: gifts given, precepts kept, kindness shown. In Sakka's heaven, Nimi is welcomed and invited to stay. And he says no. A reward he hasn't earned, he says, would be like something borrowed; he'd rather go home and do the good himself. So Matali brings him back to Mithila, and Nimi tells his people what he saw, and goes on ruling, giving, and keeping his vows. Tradition pairs this tale with the perfection of resolve, adhitthana: a decision that holds. Given a glimpse of how things end, a person might want to skip straight to the good part. Nimi uses the glimpse to go back to work. He knows where the road leads, so he walks it on purpose, and the ordinary days of ruling are where it happens.

segments.voice: Picture tonight, just before sleep, looking back over this day, and ask what you'd be glad it held: a finished task, a kind word, patience in one hard moment. Let one answer come clearly, then return to this ordinary hour and notice that this is where that ending gets made.
Adhitthana. Resolve: the perfection King Nimi showed, shown where deeds lead, who turned down a reward and went home to do good himself. Today's word.
Your line: he came back to rule. A borrowed reward was never his. Day eight hundred forty-one, done.

842.title: The prince set for sacrifice
842.hook: Candakumara, marked for a sacrifice by a wicked priest, saved by truth (Jataka 542)
842.tomorrow: The serpent who kept the precepts
842.howItsDone: The tale of Canda (also called the Khandahala Jataka) is told as an example of the perfection of patience; Buddhist ethics begins with the precept of not harming living beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adhitthana, resolve, and King Nimi, who saw where deeds lead and went home to do the work. Your line: he came back to rule. Today, a prince who stands where cruelty is about to happen.

A courtroom, and a judge who sells his verdicts. He is Khandahala, the king's chaplain, and whoever pays him wins. One day a man who has been cheated walks out weeping and meets Prince Canda, who hears the case again and gives the true verdict. The crowd cheers the prince for an honest judgment. Khandahala says nothing at all, and waits for his chance.
screen: `A JUDGE WHO TAKES BRIBES.` → `THE PRINCE HEARS IT AGAIN.` → `KHANDAHALA WAITS.`

segments.voice: The chance comes when the king dreams of heaven and asks Khandahala the way there. A great sacrifice, the chaplain says: the king's own children, queens, wealthy citizens, and animals, Prince Canda among them. Canda doesn't rage. He begs his father, reasons with him, reminds him of everything between them. The people weep in the streets. The story lets the king waver, ordering the prisoners freed, then taken back again, as Khandahala works on his fear. At the place of sacrifice, with the blade raised, Canda's wife speaks. She declares the truth of her life and asks that, by that truth, the harm be stopped. And Sakka, king of the gods, comes blazing down and terrifies the king into letting them go. The crowd turns on the chaplain, the king is driven out, and Canda is made king. Tradition pairs this tale with patience, khanti. Canda's patience isn't silence. He speaks the whole time, clearly, without hatred, to the man about to kill him. The story is about cruelty dressed up as a sacred duty, and it puts its hope in two things: a person who keeps pleading without hating, and words that are true.

segments.voice: Think of one small unkindness near you that's gone unchallenged: a joke at someone's expense, a way people talk about a coworker. Picture saying one true sentence about it, calmly, without contempt for anyone, the way Canda pleaded, and let it settle until it sounds like you.
Khanti. Patience: what Canda, marked to die for a chaplain's grudge, kept as he pleaded without hatred, before his wife's act of truth saved him. Today's word.
Your line: saved by truth. Patience, here, was never the same as silence. See you tomorrow.

843.title: The serpent who kept the precepts
843.hook: the naga prince Bhuridatta keeps the uposatha even when captured (Jataka 543)
843.howItsDone: On uposatha days, tied to the phases of the moon, Buddhist lay people may visit a temple, listen to teaching, and take extra precepts for the day and night, such as eating no food after midday.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khanti, patience, and Prince Canda pleading without hatred until true words stopped a sacrifice. Your line: saved by truth. Today, someone who keeps a vow with his life on the line.

A great snake lies coiled on top of an anthill by a river, perfectly still. He isn't hunting, and he isn't asleep. He's keeping a holy day. In the Jataka he is Bhuridatta, a prince of the nagas, the serpent beings of the waters, who has come up into the human world to keep the observance without distraction. He has made a vow about anyone who finds him there. Today, someone does.
screen: `A SNAKE ON AN ANTHILL.` → `KEEPING A HOLY DAY.` → `A VOW ABOUT ANYONE WHO COMES.`

segments.voice: The uposatha is the Buddhist observance day, when lay people take on extra precepts and keep them for the day and night. Bhuridatta's vow, the story says, is that if anyone wants his skin, his flesh, anything at all, they can take it; he won't break his precepts to stop them. Then the betrayal. A hunter who knows where he lies betrays him to a snake charmer, in a bargain over a magic jewel. The charmer seizes him and crushes him into a basket. Bhuridatta has the power to destroy his captor, the story says, with a single angry look. He won't give him even that. He keeps his eyes shut rather than look at the man in anger, so his precept holds. The charmer drags him from village to village and makes him dance for coins, and still he keeps it. At last his family searches for him, finds him, and wins him free. Tradition pairs this tale with sila, virtue. Not a show of goodness for an audience, but a line kept when breaking it would be easy and would even seem fair. The precept isn't tested on a quiet day. It's tested in the basket.

segments.voice: Pick a single precept, like not speaking falsely or not taking what isn't given, and picture the moment today when it will be hardest to keep. See yourself in that moment, holding the line quietly, the way the serpent kept his eyes closed.

Your line: he kept it. No speech, no drama, just the line, held. Day eight hundred forty-three, done.

844.title: The daughter who argued
844.hook: Princess Ruja rescues her father from a false teaching (Jataka 544)
844.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching holds that intentional actions, kamma, bear fruit; the tale of Ruja and Narada is told to show why that teaching matters for how a person lives and gives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: uposatha, the observance day, and a naga prince who kept his precepts in a snake charmer's basket. Your line: he kept it. Today, a princess who won't let her father's mistake stand.

On a bright festival night, King Angati of Mithila asks his advisers what would make the evening complete. One suggests visiting a famous ascetic. The ascetic, Guna, tells the king something that sounds like freedom: there is no fruit of deeds. Good or bad, nothing you do comes back. What will be, will be. The king goes home convinced. Today, the person who argues him out of it: his daughter.
screen: `A FESTIVAL NIGHT.` → `NO FRUIT OF DEEDS.` → `THE KING IS CONVINCED.`

segments.voice: Angati stops giving. He closes his gifts to the poor and turns to his own pleasures, since nothing, he now believes, makes a difference. Then Princess Ruja comes to him, as she regularly does, to ask for money for her own gifts. He refuses and explains his new view. And she argues. Respectfully, calling him father, but she doesn't back down. The story says she could remember past lives, and she tells him of one where a wrong she did came back to her in suffering. Deeds have fruit, she says; she has seen it. The king won't move. So Ruja turns to the directions and asks, in effect, for any good being in the world to come and help. Narada, a being from a high heaven, comes down dressed as an ascetic, and with patience and vivid pictures of where deeds lead, brings the king back to giving and to his precepts. Tradition pairs this tale with equanimity, upekkha. The one who stands up to the false teaching isn't a sage or a minister. It's a daughter, speaking up at home, to her own father, with no guarantee he'll listen. She argues with love, not contempt, and she asks for help when her own words run out. That's the shape of disagreeing well.

845.title: The wise minister
845.hook: Vidhura is won at dice by a spirit and teaches him on the way (Jataka 545)
845.howItsDone: Vidhura's story is told as an example of the perfection of truth; in Buddhist practice, sharing the teaching is valued as a gift in itself, the gift of the Dhamma.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Princess Ruja, who stood up to her father's false teaching. Your line: the daughter argued. Today, a wise man lost in a game of dice.

A stranger arrives at the king's court with a jewel and a horse that can run through the sky, and offers a game of dice. If he loses, the king takes both. If he wins, he wants one thing: the king's minister, Vidhura, known across the kingdom for his wisdom. The king rolls, and loses. The stranger is a yakkha, a fierce spirit, named Punnaka.
screen: `A JEWEL, A SKY-HORSE, DICE.` → `THE STAKE: VIDHURA.` → `THE KING LOSES.`

segments.voice: Far below, in the realm of the nagas, a queen named Vimala has heard Vidhura speak about goodness, and she longs for his heart. Her daughter, Irandati, offers to marry whoever brings it, and Punnaka sets out to get it. But he takes the word literally. On the journey, with Vidhura clinging to the horse's tail through the sky, he tries to frighten the minister to death, and finally tries to dash him from a mountaintop. Vidhura stays unshaken, and asks a calm question: why are you doing this? Punnaka tells him. Instead of pleading for his life, Vidhura teaches him how a good person lives, keeps faith with friends, and repays kindness. Punnaka is changed, and offers to take him home. Vidhura says no; take me to the nagas, as you promised. In the naga palace it comes out at last. The queen never wanted flesh. The heart she longed for was his wisdom, and Vidhura gives it, teaching the naga king and queen, and then goes home. Tradition pairs this tale with truth, sacca. Notice where the teaching happens. Not in a temple, not at court. In the hands of someone trying to kill him, on a mountaintop, on the worst day of his life. Vidhura treats even that as a place to teach.

846.title: The clever sage
846.hook: Mahosadha solves the court's riddles and saves the kingdom by wit (Jataka 546)
846.howItsDone: The Mahosadha story is told as a tale of practical wisdom; in Buddhist teaching, wisdom (panna) is one of the ten perfections.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vidhura the pandita, a wise one, who taught the spirit carrying him off. Your line: he taught his captor. Today, a boy who solves things.

Two women, one baby, and a judge who is still a child. Each woman swears the baby is hers. Nobody saw what happened. In the Jataka the judge is a village boy named Mahosadha, who has built a hall where people bring their quarrels, and this is one of them. He doesn't ask for witnesses. He draws a line on the ground.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE BABY.` → `A BOY JUDGE.` → `A LINE ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The story says he was born holding a healing herb, and so he was called Mahosadha, great medicine: a fitting name for someone whose gift is fixing things. Back to the line. He places the baby on it and tells the women to pull, one by the arms, one by the legs; whoever pulls the child across keeps him. They pull. The baby cries out. And one woman lets go, rather than hurt him. That, the boy says, is the mother. The other, the story reveals, wasn't human at all. Case after case goes like that: he finds the answer by watching how people act, not by guessing. Word reaches King Vedeha of Mithila, who brings the boy to court. There, jealous advisers test him, scheme against him, try to get him thrown out. He keeps answering riddles, keeps seeing through traps. When a rival king threatens Mithila, Mahosadha's plan, a great tunnel, the ummagga the tale is named for, turns a trap into a peace and saves his king. Tradition pairs this tale with wisdom, panna. It's a practical wisdom. It reads people, and it's always used to protect someone: the baby, the cheated, the king. The baby goes home with the woman who let go.

847.title: Vessantara, read whole
847.hook: the generous prince's tale, read from the white elephant to the homecoming (Jataka 547)
847.howItsDone: In Theravada lands the Vessantara tale is retold, chanted and painted, and some communities recite it in full at a yearly festival as a teaching on generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: panna, wisdom, and the boy judge whose wit saved a king. Your line: wit that saves. A king, a prince, a serpent, a daughter, a minister: this week's tales all lead to today's.

The elephant is white, and the people of the Sivi kingdom say it brings the rain. Envoys arrive from Kalinga, a land dried out by drought, and ask the crown prince for it. He pours water over their hands to seal the gift and hands the elephant over. By evening the city is furious, and the king is pressed to send his own son into exile. The prince is Vessantara. Tradition places his tale at the end of the Jataka and tells it as the bodhisatta's last life before the one in which he became the Buddha.
screen: `A WHITE ELEPHANT, GIVEN AWAY.` → `A CITY IN UPROAR.` → `A PRINCE SENT INTO EXILE.`

segments.voice: Vessantara leaves with his wife Maddi and their two small children, Jali and Kanhajina. He gives away his wealth before he goes, and on the road the chariot and horses too, so the family walks. They settle in huts on a mountain called Vankagiri. Then the hardest gift. An old brahmin named Jujaka, pushed by a young wife who wants servants, finds the hermitage while Maddi is out gathering fruit, and asks for the children. Vessantara gives them. What Maddi finds when she comes home belongs to tomorrow. Then the last test. The god Sakka arrives disguised as a brahmin and asks for Maddi herself. Vessantara gives her too, and Sakka at once gives her back and shows who he is. Jujaka leads the children to their grandfather, the king, who ransoms them. The whole court goes up the mountain, the family is together again, and Vessantara returns as king. In the telling, the earth shakes at his gifts. This is a hard tale, and Buddhists have said so themselves. In the Questions of King Milinda, a king asks the monk Nagasena: was giving away the children not cruel? Nagasena calls it a gift almost too great to do, made for the sake of awakening. Some readers hear in it dana, generosity, carried to its edge. Others point out that the tale never hides the cost: the children's fear and the mother's grief are told in full. Read whole, it holds the gift and what the gift costs, and it ends with everyone home.
screen: `THE ROAD OUT, ON FOOT.` · `THE HARDEST GIFT.` · `SAKKA ASKS FOR MADDI.` · `THE FAMILY HOME AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE GIFT AND WHAT IT COSTS.`

segments.voice: Pick one moment from today's tale, the white elephant handed over, the family walking without a chariot, the god giving Maddi back, the reunion on the mountain, and tell it to yourself slowly, in your own words, as if to a child at bedtime. Notice which scene you chose, and which ones you passed over.
Vessantara. The prince who gave away everything he was asked for, told as the bodhisatta's last life before the Buddha. Today's word.
